_meta.purpose: Ashoka's rule of the land, read from HIS OWN WORDS. Because the Brahmi script was deciphered (Prinsep, 1837), we can do something rare for the ancient world: verify what a ruler proclaimed and map how far his writ ran — not from later legend, but from the ~2,270-year-old edicts he had carved across the empire. The find-spots trace the reach of Mauryan authority; the texts state its ethics.
_meta.honesty: Two lines kept apart, as everywhere in this atlas. (1) HIS OWN WORDS — the edict texts, in Prakrit (Brahmi/Kharoshthi) and Greek/Aramaic on the frontier, are primary and datable; we quote translations and attribute them. (2) LATER LEGEND — the Buddhist chronicles (Ashokavadana, Mahavamsa) that make him a monster-turned-saint are later and hagiographic; we don't mix them into the edict record. The edicts are propaganda too — a king's self-image in stone — so 'what he SAID' is not automatically 'what he DID'. We present the edicts as the ruler's own declared programme, which is exactly what makes them evidence of how he wanted his rule seen.
_meta.why_the_map_matters: An edict is a fixed point: it was carved where Mauryan power could carve it. So the scatter of find-spots — from Kandahar (Afghanistan) to Karnataka, from Gujarat to Odisha to the Nepal terai — is the physical footprint of the empire. Where the script CHANGES (Brahmi in the core, Kharoshthi in the northwest, Greek & Aramaic at the Hellenistic frontier) you are reading the multilingual EDGE of Mauryan rule.

ruler.name: Ashoka (Aśoka) Maurya
ruler.note: For a long time the edicts' 'Devānāṃpiya Piyadasi' was not firmly tied to 'Ashoka' — the Maski and Gujarra minor edicts, which give the name Aśoka directly, clinched the identification.

sources.label: Edicts of Ashoka — Wikipedia (find-spots, scripts, contents)
Major Rock Edicts — Wikipedia; trans. E. Hultzsch, 'Inscriptions of Asoka' (1925, public domain)

scripts_legend.label: Brahmi
scripts_legend.note: The Mauryan state script — most edicts, left-to-right, ancestor of nearly all later Indian scripts.

scripts_legend.label: Kharoshthi
scripts_legend.note: Aramaic-derived, right-to-left; used at Shahbazgarhi & Mansehra in the northwest frontier.

scripts_legend.label: Greek
scripts_legend.note: At Kandahar, for the Greek-speaking population of the former Achaemenid/Seleucid borderland.

scripts_legend.label: Aramaic
scripts_legend.note: The old Achaemenid administrative language, still current on the far northwest — Kandahar, Taxila, Laghman.

sites.name: Kandahar
sites.note: The far NORTHWEST limit. A bilingual Greek–Aramaic edict for the Hellenistic populace — proof Mauryan authority reached beyond the Hindu Kush.

sites.name: Shahbazgarhi
sites.note: Major Rock Edicts in Kharoshthi — the northwest, written right-to-left in the region's own script.

sites.name: Mansehra
sites.note: The other great Kharoshthi rock-edict site of the northwest.

sites.name: Taxila
sites.note: Aramaic inscription — the old Achaemenid tongue lingering on the frontier.

sites.name: Girnar (Junagadh)
sites.note: One of the most complete sets of all 14 Major Rock Edicts, in Brahmi — the western anchor.

sites.name: Sopara
sites.note: Fragmentary Major Rock Edicts on the west coast — Mauryan reach to the Konkan ports.

sites.name: Kalsi
sites.note: Major Rock Edicts in the Himalayan foothills — the northern core.

sites.name: Dhauli
sites.note: In conquered KALINGA itself. Carries the two 'Separate Edicts' addressed to the newly-subjugated people — a softer administrative tone. Near the war Ashoka came to regret.

sites.name: Jaugada
sites.note: The other Kalinga site with the Separate Edicts — governance of the freshly conquered land.

sites.name: Yerragudi
sites.note: Both Major AND Minor Rock Edicts, deep in the Deccan — the southern reach.

sites.name: Sannati
sites.note: Rare Major Rock Edicts in the far south — including a version of the Separate Edicts.

sites.name: Maski
sites.note: CRUCIAL: a Minor Rock Edict that names 'Aśoka' directly — the find that firmly tied the edicts' 'Devānāṃpiya' to the historical Ashoka.

sites.name: Gujarra
sites.note: Also names 'Ashoka' explicitly — the second key identity clue.

sites.name: Brahmagiri
sites.note: Minor Rock Edict in southern Karnataka — the deep-south administrative frontier.

sites.name: Bairat (Bhabru)
sites.note: The Bhabru edict — Ashoka addresses the Buddhist sangha directly, recommending specific texts: his personal faith on record.

sites.name: Sasaram
sites.note: Minor Rock Edict near the Magadhan heartland.

sites.name: Barabar Caves
sites.note: Rock-cut caves Ashoka DEDICATED to the Ajivika ascetics — carved dedication inscriptions; evidence of his patronage across sects, not only Buddhists.

sites.name: Delhi–Topra pillar
sites.note: Carries the full set of 7 Major Pillar Edicts — Ashoka's mature statement of dhamma. Later moved to Delhi by Firuz Shah Tughlaq.

sites.name: Allahabad (Kausambi) pillar
sites.note: Pillar Edicts + the 'Queen's Edict' + (later) the Schism Edict warning against splitting the sangha.

sites.name: Lauria Nandangarh pillar
sites.note: A near-complete polished sandstone pillar with the Major Pillar Edicts — the Mauryan north.

sites.name: Rampurva pillar
sites.note: Pillars with bull & lion capitals bearing the Pillar Edicts, near the Nepal border.

sites.name: Lumbini pillar
sites.note: Marks the BIRTHPLACE OF THE BUDDHA; records Ashoka's visit and his TAX RELIEF for the village — a dated act of rule, not legend: he cut Lumbini's land-tax to 1/8.

sites.name: Nigali Sagar pillar
sites.note: Records Ashoka enlarging the stupa of an earlier Buddha — pilgrimage-building by the state.

sites.name: Sarnath pillar
sites.note: The pillar whose LION CAPITAL is now India's national emblem; carries the Schism Edict. Where the Buddha first taught.

sites.name: Sanchi pillar
sites.note: Pillar with the Schism Edict beside the great stupa — state and sangha side by side.

edicts.theme: No animal slaughter / end of the feast-kill
edicts.summary: Bans animal sacrifice and festive gatherings; Ashoka records cutting the daily kill in the royal kitchen from many thousands to two peacocks and a deer, and aims for none.
Medical care for humans AND animals, medicinal herbs planted, wells dug and shade-trees set along roads — even in the lands of neighbouring kings (the Cholas, Pandyas, and 'Antiyoka the Greek king').
Administrative order that officials tour the realm every five years to teach dhamma alongside their duties: governance as moral instruction.
Where kings once sounded the war-drum (bherī-ghosa), Ashoka now sounds the 'drum of dhamma' (dhamma-ghosa) — the reign's programme in one image.
Creates a new cadre of 'dhamma officers' to look after the welfare and fair treatment of all sects, prisoners, the aged, and border peoples.
Ashoka orders that reports reach him at ALL times, wherever he is — eating, in the harem, walking — because 'I am never content with my exertion': an ideology of the ever-available ruler.
Wishes that people of ALL religious sects may live in all places, seeking self-control and purity of heart — a charter of coexistence.
Instead of royal hunting/pleasure tours (vihāra-yātrā), Ashoka now makes 'dhamma tours' (dhamma-yātrā) — visiting the people, elders and ascetics.

edicts.theme: True ceremony is conduct, not ritual
edicts.summary: Downplays showy rituals (especially those women perform); the ceremony that bears fruit is right conduct toward servants, elders, animals and ascetics.
Ashoka rejects glory and fame as ends in themselves; the only worthwhile renown is that people follow dhamma.

edicts.theme: The gift of dhamma is the best gift
edicts.summary: The 'gift of dhamma' — right relations among people — surpasses every material gift, and spreads without limit.

edicts.theme: Honour other sects — restrain your own praise
edicts.summary: A striking plea for religious restraint: honour other sects, and do NOT over-praise your own or disparage others, 'for whoever praises his own sect... harms his own sect'.

The famous edict: the conquest of Kalinga, its terrible toll, Ashoka's remorse, and his turn from conquest-by-arms to 'conquest by dhamma' — even naming the Hellenistic kings (Antiochus, Ptolemy, Antigonus, Magas, Alexander) among whom he claims dhamma has spread.
A closing note that the edicts exist in short, medium and long forms, engraved across the vast empire so all may see — the edicts explaining themselves.
Protection through dhamma, self-examination, and the fear of sin as the guard of good government.

A remarkable conservation LAW: lists dozens of protected animals and birds, bans castration and branding on certain days, and forbids killing on numerous holy days — arguably the world's earliest wildlife-protection statute.
Ashoka's retrospective: the dhamma-officers, the planted trees and wells, and his hope that his sons and great-grandsons will continue the work 'as long as the moon and sun endure'.
At Dhauli & Jaugada in Kalinga: officers told to treat ALL subjects as the king's own children, to avoid harshness and wrongful imprisonment — the administrative face of the post-war turn.

edicts.theme: Tax relief at the Buddha's birthplace
edicts.summary: At Lumbini: Ashoka, on visiting the Buddha's birthplace, exempts the village from the bali tax and fixes its land-revenue share at one-eighth — a concrete, dated act of taxation policy carved in stone.

kalinga.title: Major Rock Edict 13 — the Kalinga war and the ruler's remorse
kalinga.when: war c. 261–260 BCE (8th regnal year); edict carved c. 256–255 BCE
kalinga.quote_conquest: When King Beloved-of-the-Gods, Priyadarsin, had been anointed eight years, (the country of) the Kalingas was conquered by (him). One hundred and fifty thousand in number were the men who were deported thence, one hundred thousand in number were those who were slain there, and many times as many those who died.
kalinga.quote_remorse: After that, now that (the country of) the Kalingas has been taken, Beloved-of-the-Gods (is devoted) to a zealous study of morality (Dharma), to the love of morality, and to the instruction (of people) in morality. This is the repentance of Beloved-of-the-Gods on account of his conquest of (the country of) the Kalingas.
kalinga.translator: trans. E. Hultzsch, 'Inscriptions of Asoka' (1925, public domain)
kalinga.significance: The rarest thing in the ancient record: a victorious emperor publishing his own regret at the human cost of his victory, and pledging a change of policy — carved not once but repeated across the empire. It is the strongest single reason the edicts are read as more than boast.
